Its proof: "We know that Theta(z) is real and entire of order 1/2. All of its derivatives ... implies that Theta^{(n)}(z) is real and entire of genus 1* for all n >= 0."

Therefore Phi.Omega is in the Laguerre-Polya class if and only if Phi(z) is hyperbolic." Attributing it to Lemma 3.4 drops that hypothesis. Numbering (3.3)/(3.5) matches v2.

results.claim: THEOREM 3.12: the k-point un-averaged Chowla statement E_{n<=X} lambda(n+h_1)...lambda(n+h_k)=o(1) holds for k odd or k=2, for all scales X outside a set of zero logarithmic density; and (separately) correlations of bounded multiplicative functions vanish at almost all scales with an explicit structure theorem (vanish unless g_1...g_k weakly pretends to be a twisted Dirichlet character n -> chi(n)n^{it}).

results.claim: The k=1 case of the Chowla conjecture, sum_{n<=x} lambda(n) = o(x), is equivalent to the prime number theorem and is therefore a theorem, not open; quoted to Tao arXiv:1605.04628 Sec. 1.
results.paper_quote: Sec. 1 (Introduction), unnumbered prose, p. 2: "The $k=1$ case of the Chowla conjecture is equivalent to the prime number theorem. The higher $k$ cases are open, although there are a number of partial results available if one allows for some averaging in the $b_{1},\dots,b_{k}$ parameters..."
results.doc_quote: *"The `k=1` case of the Chowla conjecture is equivalent to the prime number theorem. The higher `k` cases are open."*
results.notes: Quote check: first sentence verbatim; the second sentence is truncated at "open" and the paper's comma becomes a period (paper continues ", although there are a number of partial results available ..."). results.claim: Correction row X1: the round's claim that one-point Chowla sum_{n<=x} lambda(n) = o(x) is OPEN is false; it is equivalent to PNT, i.e. a theorem, via lambda = 1_squares * mu giving sum_{n<=x} lambda(n) = sum_{d<=sqrt(x)} M(x/d^2) = o(x) from M(y) = o(y); cited to Tao arXiv:1605.04628 (with MRT arXiv:1509.01545).

results.claim: THEOREM 3.6: there is an absolute δ>0 with Σ_{n≤x} λ(n)λ(n+1) ≪ (1−δ)x, giving no decay, with the shift h=1; quoted from the abstract (third consequence) of Matomäki–Radziwiłł arXiv:1501.04585.

This settles an old folklore conjecture and constitutes progress towards Chowla's conjecture." Numbered form, Corollary 2: "For every integer h ≥ 1, there exists δ(h) > 0 such that (1/X)|Σ_{n≤X} λ(n)λ(n+h)| ≤ 1 − δ(h) for all large enough X > 1."

This settles an old folklore conjecture and constitutes progress towards Chowla's conjecture."

results.claim: Row T5, two clauses: (a) Σ_{n≤x} λ(n)λ(n+1) ≪ (1−δ)x for some δ>0; (b) μ cancels in almost all short intervals [x, x+ψ(x)] with ψ(x) → ∞ arbitrarily slowly, i.e. the Möbius sum over the interval is o of its length for almost every x.

Corollary 2: "For every integer h ≥ 1, there exists δ(h) > 0 such that (1/X)|Σ_{n≤X} λ(n)λ(n+h)| ≤ 1 − δ(h) for all large enough X > 1."

Clause (a) is the abstract's third consequence / Corollary 2 (δ = δ(h) in general; h = 1 gives an absolute constant, exactly the shift the row uses). Clause (b) is the abstract's first consequence verbatim; the quantitative engine is Theorem 1 with f = μ, whose exceptional set C·X((log h)^{1/3}/(δ²h^{δ/25}) + 1/(δ²(log X)^{1/50})) is o(X) as h = ψ(x) → ∞, so "almost every x" and "arbitrarily slowly" are faithful. results.claim: THEOREM 3.8: Tao's arXiv:1509.05422 result holds for k = 2 and every fixed affine pair with a_1b_2 − a_2b_1 ≠ 0, in particular (1/log x) Σ_{n≤x} λ(n)λ(n+2)/n = o(1); the parity barrier is broken only in the logarithmically averaged sense; the entropy decrement method rests on MR arXiv:1501.04585 on short intervals.

Let 1 ≤ ω(x) ≤ x be a quantity depending on x that goes to infinity as x → ∞. Then Σ_{x/ω(x)<n≤x} λ(a_1n+b_1)λ(a_2n+b_2)/n = o(log ω(x)) as n → ∞." results.claim: THEOREM 2.1(d) 'explicit published instance': Polymath8b prove that, even under GEH, the best a purely sieve-theoretic argument can reach for an admissible triple is 'at least two of n+h_1, n+h_2, n+h_3 are prime', and that this is optimal for sieve-theoretic considerations. The file also quotes the abstract verbatim for the optimality sentence.

Sec. 8: 'the "parity barrier" of Selberg prohibits sieve-theoretic methods ... from obtaining any bound on H_1 that is stronger than H_1 <= 6, even on the assumption of ... GEH ... and even if one uses sieves other than the Selberg sieve.' Also Theorem 1.4(xii)/3.2(xii): DHL[3,2] under GEH[theta], 0<theta<1.

results.claim: Calls it THEOREM 3.11 (its own number), citing MRTT arXiv:1503.05121 for: for fixed k and H=H(x)<=x with H(x)->inf, sum_{h_1,...,h_k<=H} |sum_{n<=x} lambda(n+h_1)...lambda(n+h_k)| = o(H^k x); consequently sum_{n<=x} lambda(n)lambda(n+h) = o(x) for almost every shift h<=H(x), for any H(x)->inf; and the same paper gives int_0^X |sum_{x<=n<=x+H} lambda(n)e(alpha n)| dx = o(HX) uniformly in alpha. The document labels the source READ as 'abstract verified verbatim' (Appendix A row MRT1, via arXiv API).
results.paper_quote: Theorem 1.1 (Chowla's conjecture on average). For any natural number k, and any 10 <= H <= X, we have sum_{1<=h_1,...,h_k<=H} |sum_{1<=n<=X} lambda(n+h_1)...lambda(n+h_k)| << k ( log log H / log H + 1/log^{1/3000} X ) H^k X. (1.2) ... Theorem 1.3 (Exponential sum estimate). For any 10 <= H <= X, one has sup_{alpha in R} int_0^X |sum_{x<=n<=x+H} lambda(n)e(alpha n)| dx << ( log log H / log H + 1/log^{1/700} X ) H X.  [Abstract:] ...= o(H^k X) as X -> inf whenever H = H(X) <= X goes to infinity as X -> inf, and k is fixed.
results.doc_quote: For fixed `k` and `H = H(x) ≤ x` with `H(x) → ∞`, `Σ_{h_1,…,h_k ≤ H} | Σ_{n≤x} λ(n+h_1) ⋯ λ(n+h_k) | = o(H^k x)`. In particular the two-point correlation `Σ_{n≤x} λ(n)λ(n+h)` is `o(x)` for **almost every** shift `h ≤ H(x)`, for any `H(x) → ∞`. The same paper gives `∫_0^X |Σ_{x≤n≤x+H} λ(n) e(αn)| dx = o(HX)` uniformly in `α`.
results.notes: Read full v3 HTML (01 Mar 2022); abs page and v1/v2 abstracts identical, so no numbering conflict. Attribution and content otherwise right: display 1 = paper's Theorem 1.1/abstract (its wording), display 2 = Theorem 1.3 (given there as sup_alpha = 'uniformly in alpha'), 'almost every shift' follows by Markov. Dropped: (i) the explicit error terms of (1.2) and Thm 1.3 (loglogH/logH + log^{-1/3000}X resp. log^{-1/700}X), the paper's quantitative content, advertised in its abstract; (ii) the hypothesis 10 <= H <= X. The o(.) reading stays legitimate since H->inf makes both o(1), so the claim is not false, only weaker than the source. No version is recorded in Status.

results.claim: THEOREM 3.8: Tao (arXiv:1509.05422) proves the log-averaged two-point Chowla statement for k = 2 and every fixed affine pair with a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1 != 0; in particular (1/log x) * sum_{n<=x} lambda(n)lambda(n+2)/n = o(1). The doc records Definition 3.7's hypotheses: omega = omega(x) -> infinity with omega(x) <= x, and that the result breaks the parity barrier only in the logarithmically averaged sense, not the un-averaged one.
results.paper_quote: Theorem 1.2 (Logarithmically averaged Chowla conjecture). Let a_1,a_2 be natural numbers, and let b_1,b_2 be integers such that a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1 != 0. Let 1 <= omega(x) <= x be a quantity depending on x that goes to infinity as x -> infinity. Then one has sum_{x/omega(x)<n<=x} lambda(a_1 n + b_1) lambda(a_2 n + b_2)/n = o(log omega(x))  (1.3) as n -> infinity.
results.doc_quote: THEOREM 3.8 (log-averaged two-point Chowla; Tao 2015/2016). Definition 3.7 holds for `k = 2` and every fixed affine pair with `a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1 != 0`. In particular `(1/log x) sum_{n<=x} lambda(n) lambda(n+2)/n = o(1)`.
results.notes: Read as PDF (v4, 29 Jul 2016, 32 pp.), cross-checked against the v4 TeX source; the HTML page truncated before the statement, so the PDF was decisive. Numbering mismatch: the paper has no Theorem 3.8; the result is Theorem 1.2, eq. (1.3), and '3.8' is the archive's own dictionary number. Hypotheses match exactly. The doc's 'in particular' instance takes a_1=1,b_1=0,a_2=1,b_2=2, so a_1b_2-a_2b_1=2 != 0: non-degeneracy holds. Scope faithful (parity barrier claimed only for the log-averaged problem). Numbering is version-stable: v1 and v4 both Theorem 1.2. Abstract quote verbatim; venue appears only in the arXiv comment field, so the doc's hedge is accurate.

results.claim: The archive row X1 had called one-point Chowla (sum_{n<=x} lambda(n) = o(x)) OPEN; the document corrects this to: it is a theorem, equivalent to PNT (Mertens form M(y) = o(y)), via lambda = 1_squares * mu giving sum_{n<=x} lambda(n) = sum_{d<=sqrt(x)} M(x/d^2) = o(x). It also cites Tao arXiv:1605.04628 as the source and Matomaki-Radziwill-Tao arXiv:1509.01545 sec. 1 as an additional reference.
results.paper_quote: MRT 1509.01545 (read as HTML, v2), introduction after Conjecture 1.3 (Chowla): "For k = 1, this claim is equivalent to the prime number theorem, but for k > 1 Chowla's conjecture remains open." Tao 1605.04628 (read as HTML), introduction after Conjecture 1.1: "The k = 1 case of the Chowla conjecture is equivalent to the prime number theorem. The higher k cases are open" and "lambda(n) = sum_{d^2|n} mu(n/d^2)". No numbered theorem: both are unnumbered remarks in sec. 1.
results.doc_quote: "**false** -- it is **equivalent to PNT**, i.e. a **theorem**.  `lambda = 1_squares * mu`, so `Σ_{n≤x}lambda(n) = Σ_{d≤√x} M(x/d²) = o(x)` follows from `M(y) = o(y)`"; Status: "CITED (literature; `λ = 1_squares ∗ μ`, cited Tao [arXiv:1605.04628](...))".
results.notes: Both statements are unnumbered introduction remarks, so no numbering mismatch. Batch paper 1509.01545: v1 2015-09-04, v2 2015-09-23; only v2 exists and its HTML was read. The archive's own citation is Tao 1605.04628 (v1 only), read too; it gives the same sentence, so the attribution is faithful. k=1 Chowla with a_1=1,b_1=0 is exactly sum_{n<=x} lambda(n)=o(x); both papers treat k>1 (incl. sum lambda(n)lambda(n+2)) as open, as the document says. Paper prints the identity as lambda(n)=sum_{d^2|n} mu(n/d^2), equivalent to the document's convolution form. The witness (x=100,1000) is the document's own computation, not a citation; reproduced: L(100)=-2, L(1000)=-14, matching sum_d M(x/d^2).

results.claim: Cassaigne's first-difference method (Complexity and special factors, Bull. SMF 125 (1997) 1-26, Zbl 0921.68065) gives p(L+1)-p(L) = sum_{f in F(L)}(d+(f)-1) for an extendable language with d+ >= 1, so HANDOFF 3.4's form p(L+1)-p(L) = #right-special is correct only there; the right-special/extendability framework is as in Cassaigne-Nicolas, arXiv:0903.1627.
results.paper_quote: 0903.1627v5 Def. 1: 'We say that a word w in A* is a (right-)special factor of the language L if there exist a, b in A with a != b such that both wa and wb are factors of L.' Def. 2: 'We say that the language L is (right-)extendable if for each w in L, there exists a in A such that wa in L.' The identity is in the work the Status names: Cassaigne, 'Complexite et facteurs speciaux' (Zbl 0921.68065), Prop. 3.4 (OCR): 'Soit L un langage factoriel prolongeable. Alors sum_{u in L inter A^n} m_d(u) = sum m_g(u) = p(n+1) - p(n)', with m_d(u) = #{x in A^k : ux in L} - 1 = d+(u) - 1.
results.doc_quote: Cassaigne's first-difference method (Complexity and special factors, Bull. SMF 125 (1997) 1-26, Zbl 0921.68065) gives p(L+1)-p(L)=sum_{f in F(L)}(d+(f)-1) for an *extendable* language, where d+>=1, so HANDOFF 3.4's form p(L+1)-p(L)=#right-special is correct only there; right-special/extendability as in [Cassaigne-Nicolas, arXiv:0903.1627].
results.notes: Read 0903.1627v5 HTML + v5 LaTeX source: it defines right-special (Def. 1) and extendable (Def. 2) exactly as used, but has no equality; its closing section-3 exercise (Ex. 8, v5) gives only p(n+1)-p(n) <= (alpha-1)s(n), and >= s(n) if L is extendable. The equality is Prop. 3.4 of the paper the Status names: Zbl 0921.68065 = Bull. Belg. Math. Soc. Simon Stevin 4 (1997) 67-88, not Bull. SMF 125 (1997) 1-26. Caveats: the paper needs L factorial and prolongeable, the doc only extendable; the unweighted #right-special form is Prop. 3.1, stated 'alphabet binaire', and order >1 factors count with multiplicity, so #RS = sum(d+-1) needs d+ <= 2. Source read via OCR of the EMIS/Wayback scan.
